situation: A week ago the user started three new skincare products at once, and their face now stings. They know the timing and the symptom; they do not yet know which product, or which ingredient, is responsible, or whether the cause is irritation, an allergy, a damaged skin barrier, or something unrelated like weather or another change in routine. Whether the stinging is mild or severe, and whether there is redness, swelling, or rash, is the decisive unknown. If it is severe or spreading, a clinician matters more than detective work. The three below are fictional voices for thinking it through, not medical advice.

minds.title: The Experimenter
minds.concern: Turning a vague suspicion into a test that could actually point at one culprit.
minds.author: Karl Popper

minds.title: The Skeptic of Stories
minds.concern: Noticing how quickly the mind picks a culprit that feels right and then stops checking.
minds.author: Daniel Kahneman

minds.title: The Subtractor
minds.concern: Reducing what is being done to the skin before adding any new investigation or fix.
minds.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: Stop all three products today and use only a gentle cleanser and plain moisturizer. Your skin is already telling you it is overloaded. Adding detective work to an irritated face is how people end up with a fourth problem.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Agreed on stopping, but stopping everything tells you only that the stinging fades. It does not tell you which product caused it. Once calm, reintroduce one product at a time, a few days apart. A culprit that returns the sting on demand is a culprit that could have been proven innocent, and wasn't.
debate.author: Karl Popper
debate.basis: Basis: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery

debate.speaker: The Skeptic of Stories
debate.text: Before you test, notice that you probably already have a suspect, likely the one with the strongest-sounding ingredient. That feels like knowledge but it is a story built from whatever came to mind first. Your test should be designed to embarrass your favorite suspect, not flatter it.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: I'd push back on the rush to retest. A reaction can leave skin more sensitive for days or weeks, so a retest too soon may sting from the leftover damage and blame an innocent product. Waiting until the skin is truly calm is part of the method, not a delay from it.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Fair, and that sharpens my claim: a test only counts if the baseline is clean. I'd add a rule that only one thing changes at a time, and that the first patch test goes on a small spot like the inner forearm or behind the ear, not the whole face.
debate.author: Karl Popper
debate.basis: Basis: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery

debate.speaker: The Skeptic of Stories
debate.text: Here is a reading the user can reject. They bought three products with hope and money, and part of them wants a clean villain so the rest of the routine can survive. Or maybe they fear the stinging means lasting damage and want a culprit mainly to feel the problem is contained.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: I'd contest that. Nothing in their words says they are attached to the routine. They asked how to figure out the cause, which fits a person who simply wants the sting to stop and would happily drop all three. Then the right answer is less ritual: skip the full investigation and keep the simple routine.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Those two readings lead to different advice. If they want the products to work, the slow one-at-a-time test is worth it, because it can rescue two of three. If they only want comfort, a long test is poor value. And if either path shows swelling, hives, or burning that spreads, the experiment ends and a clinician takes over.
debate.author: Karl Popper
debate.basis: Basis: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery

debate.speaker: The Skeptic of Stories
debate.text: I'll concede the safety point, and add a limit on all of us: even a clean test can mislead if sun, a new detergent, a cold wind, or a hot shower changes at the same moment. A rerun that gives the same sting twice is stronger than one result, however convincing the first felt.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Subtractor
debate.text: Then we land on a plan with one disagreement left. Pause everything, let the skin settle, then bring products back singly and keep a simple note of dates and reactions. I still say the user may reasonably decide the answer is not worth chasing, and I'd go further than Taleb on that: the kept products should be the ones they would miss.
debate.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

clearer: The main insight is that the order matters: calm the skin first, then test one change at a time, because a vague suspicion and an irritated baseline can both produce a confident but wrong answer. Still disputed is how much investigation the user needs: the Experimenter values a clear answer that can save good products, while the Subtractor thinks dropping the products may serve them just as well. The user might reflect on whether they are mostly hoping to rescue the routine, to be reassured the sting is not lasting, or simply to feel comfortable again, since those lead to different choices.
dependsOn: If the stinging is severe, or comes with swelling, hives, spreading redness, blistering, or trouble breathing, stop everything and get medical help rather than testing at home, because a clinician can tell an allergy from irritation and the experiment adds risk. If it is mild and fading once you stop the products, a slow reintroduction becomes reasonable: wait until skin is calm, then add one product at a time, a few days apart, starting with a small patch area, and note dates and reactions. If you mainly want comfort and do not much care about the products, keeping a simple routine and skipping the investigation becomes more reasonable, because the information is worth less to you than the risk of re-irritating your skin. If the sting does not ease after a week or two of a minimal routine, the cause may not be the products, and a dermatologist is the proportionate way to find out.
